headline: Double Creek fluke keep coming steady — weakfish deep, snappers everywhere in between
subhead: Warm, stable water has settled into a real August pattern on the bay, with the best fish coming off moving current and the last hour of light.
body_markdown:
I remember an August back in the late '80s, running a charter out of Forked River with two brothers from Pennsylvania who'd never seen a snapper blue in their lives. We anchored up near the mouth of Oyster Creek on the last of the incoming, dropped tiny bucktails tipped with spearing, and those boys couldn't reel fast enough. That's the thing about this bay in high summer — it doesn't need to be complicated. The water's warm, the bait's thick, and if you fish the moving tide instead of the dead slack, something's usually willing.

That's exactly the pattern I'm seeing right now, and it's the same one we called last week — stable, warm, southwest-wind conditions keeping the bite concentrated on the moving water rather than spread out all day. It's held. Mornings have been quiet on the slack, then the tide turns and the rods start bending.

Fluke are still the most dependable thing going. Double Creek Channel has been the play — that stretch where the sand humps up between the deeper cuts. Drift it on the last two hours of the ebb with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail and a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp trailer, bounced right on bottom in 12 to 18 feet. I've had keepers to 5 pounds mixed with a lot of shorts — call it one keeper for every four or five fish over the rail, which is honest summer math, not a blitz. Squid strips on the hook of the bucktail have been outproducing plain Gulp when the current's really moving, probably because the scent holds up better against the push.

Weakfish haven't disappeared, but they're not the shallow sedge-bank fish you find in May. Right now they're sitting deep — the channel edges off Tices Shoal and the deeper bend below Barnegat Light have given up a few 16- to 18-inch weakfish on the last of the outgoing, mostly to guys drifting bucktails tipped with a sliver of fresh spearing or working the bottom slow with a Fin-S rigged on a light jighead. It's not a numbers game right now. It's a bonus fish while you're fluking, and I'd treat it that way.

Snapper blues are the story for anybody with a kid on the boat or a light spinning rod they want to bend. They're everywhere in the back bay right now — off the docks in Toms River, along the bulkheads near Forked River, up into the mouth of Oyster Creek where the water still runs a touch warmer than the open bay even in summer. Tiny gold spoons, small Kastmasters, or a strip of bunker on a snapper rig under a bobber will get bit within minutes on the top of the tide. It's not glamorous fishing but it's the kind that keeps people coming back to this bay for forty years, same as it did for me.

Bigger bluefish are a different animal, and there's real reason for optimism there. The word up and down the Jersey coast has been a fresh wave of blues pushing south, and I expect that to start showing at Barnegat Inlet and along the Island Beach surf line any day now — bigger fish mixed into what's already a strong resident population. If you're throwing metal off the beach at Island Beach State Park, work it right at first light before the sun gets high, because these August blues feed hard early and then go quiet once the water starts to heat up on the surface.

Striped bass are where things get honest. With surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s through the bay, the bass have gone deep and mostly nocturnal — this isn't unique to us, it's the whole coast right now. Daytime bass fishing in the bay in August is mostly a waste of gas unless you're working the deepest holes with something big and slow. Your better bet is the night bite: anchor on a channel edge near Oyster Creek or the deeper water off Double Creek after dark, soak a bunker chunk or a live eel on the bottom, and be patient. It's not the May run, but a 28- to 34-inch bass at 10 p.m. on a calm night is a real thing right now for guys willing to sit still.

Blowfish are thick on the sod banks along the west side of the bay — clam on a small hook, light sinker, drop it right along the bank edges on the last of the falling tide, and you can fill a bucket in an hour if you've got the patience for it. Kingfish have been scattered but present on the ocean side, mostly in the surf troughs at Island Beach on bloodworm or Fishbites, better on the smaller incoming tides than the bigger pushes.

Watch the afternoons — this is peak thunderstorm season, and I've had more than one trip get cut short by a wall of black cloud rolling in off the Pine Barrens around 3 or 4 p.m. When that happens, the bite shuts down hard for a couple hours and then usually comes back strong on the evening tide once things settle. Plan around it rather than fighting it.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon, and I expect the current to get a little more authority behind it over the next several days — that usually sharpens up the fluke bite on the channel drifts and can trigger a better push of bass activity if a front comes through and knocks the surface temps down even a couple degrees. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of an evening ebb on Double Creek for fluke, then sit on Oyster Creek after dark for bass. That's where I'd put my money.
